cards.pitch: A deeply active, released local-first agent workspace that remains only moderately discovered.

case.text: Holon combines continuous agent workspaces, explicit task/wait models, event-driven wake-up, trust boundaries, and local-first execution, with both TUI and web GUI workflows.
Its quality score is 81.4 while popularity is just 45.8; the repository reports 981 recent commits, 77 releases, and a commit on the as-of date.

risks.text: The product is a relatively broad assistant platform, so adoption may depend on users wanting its particular local daemon, task model, and provider setup.

proven_wrong_if: Its quality-adjusted adoption fails to grow despite sustained releases and active contributions.
The local-first workspace model does not retain users beyond experimentation.

cards.pitch: A remarkably polished, almost undiscovered Rust toolkit that solves concrete rekordbox-to-CDJ workflow gaps.

case.text: Bake'n Deck has a sharply defined use case: measured loudness gain, compound key+BPM sorting, CDJ-safe transcoding, and direct USB export without replacing rekordbox.
It is the strongest popularity/quality mismatch in the shortlist: popularity 4.2 versus quality 80.6, alongside 65 releases and 53,762 README characters.

risks.text: The addressable audience is specialized and depends on rekordbox exports and Pioneer CDJ workflows; the README explicitly positions it as a supplement rather than a replacement for rekordbox.

proven_wrong_if: Usage expands beyond a niche DJ audience into a durable general music-library tool.
Real-world CDJ compatibility and release cadence continue without serious regressions.

cards.pitch: A fast-rising interoperability layer for carrying AI coding sessions across agents, with Rust, JavaScript, WASM, and CLI surfaces.

case.text: txcript converts and searches agent sessions across harnesses, offers native CLI operations such as continue/query/view/crop/export, and exposes Rust, JavaScript, and WASM interfaces.
It pairs momentum 77.1 and newness 83.3 with only 205 stars; the repository also reports nine recent commit authors and a commit on the as-of date.

risks.text: Cross-agent fidelity is inherently uneven: the README qualifies continuation by whether the target supports the carried-over information, and supported harness formats can change.

proven_wrong_if: Major coding-agent vendors converge on incompatible formats that txcript cannot keep up with.
The project gains stars but not repeat usage across multiple agent harnesses.

cards.pitch: A focused, well-released session supervisor that gives coding agents durable PTYs, browser access, and human-in-the-loop control.

case.text: Open Relay keeps the daemon-owned PTY alive after terminal closure, provides terminal and password-protected browser dashboards, supports intervention, and routes work across connected machines.
It has only 109 stars but quality 69.9, 508 commits in 90 days, six recent authors, and 35 releases.

risks.text: The README labels the 0.5.0-beta.3 channel as a breaking preview while stable installs remain on the 0.3 line, so upgrades may require migration care.

proven_wrong_if: The beta-to-stable transition causes enough breakage or churn that users abandon the supervisor.
Persistent sessions and remote intervention do not become a recurring need for agent users.

cards.pitch: A very low-star, security-conscious MCP/LSP bridge that gives AI agents real compiler and IDE semantics instead of guesses.

case.text: mcpls bridges MCP to LSP and exposes 31 tools for type information, references, diagnostics, refactoring, hierarchies, formatting, and symbol search across language servers.
Its popularity is only 16.7, yet quality is 62.0 with 210 recent commits, five recent authors, 20 releases, and a documented security/trust model.

risks.text: Language servers execute workspace code and are not sandboxed; the README explicitly warns users to consult its security guidance before analyzing untrusted code.

proven_wrong_if: MCP clients do not adopt richer compiler-aware workflows beyond basic text retrieval.
The unsandboxed language-server model blocks safe deployment in the environments that need it most.

summary: Five Rust developer-tool sleepers stand out. Holon is the best overall quality compounder; baken is the clearest extreme value/visibility mismatch; txcript is the strongest rising interoperability bet; open-relay is a practical session-supervision utility; and mcpls is the most neglected technical specialist. Muxin, pixtuoid, ttfx, Cydonia, and idx are credible alternatives, but their popularity, narrower scope, or lower quality scores weaken the sleeper case.
